pages.name: Feed in 2
pages.task: If 2 goes into the same machine, what comes out?
pages.why: `2 × 3` makes 6, and `6 − 1` makes 5. The steps go in the order the rule says.

pages.name: f of 5
pages.text: Call this machine `f`. Then `f(5)`, said "f of 5", is the output when 5 goes in, so `f(5) = 14`; the bracket holds the input and does not mean `f` times 5. The whole rule is `f(x) = 3x − 1`, where `x`, the input you choose, is the [[independent variable]], and `f(x)` is the [[dependent variable]], because it depends on `x`.

pages.name: Feed in a + 1
pages.task: Whatever goes in the bracket replaces `x`, all of it at once. If `a + 1` goes in, what is `f(a + 1)`?
pages.why: `f(a + 1) = 3(a + 1) − 1`, which is `3a + 3 − 1`, so `3a + 2`. Try `a = 2`. The input is then 3, and `f(3) = 8`, which `3a + 2` makes too.

pages.name: Is the log a function?
pages.task: Hours 2 and 3 both read 15 A. Is this log a function?
pages.why: Each hour has exactly one reading, so each input gives one output. Hours 2 and 3 sharing 15 A is fine, because they are two different inputs.

pages.name: Two outputs
pages.text: The rule "a number that squares to make it" gives 16 two outputs, 4 and −4. One input with two outputs is not a function. The square root, √, keeps only the 4, and that is a function.

pages.name: The 4 to 20 mA loop
pages.task: A transmitter turns a reading `p`, in percent, into a current by `S(p) = 0.16p + 4`, so 0% sends 4 mA and 100% sends 20 mA. What is `S(50)`?
pages.why: `S(50) = 0.16 × 50 + 4`. That is `8 + 4`, so 12 mA, halfway between 4 and 20 mA.

pages.name: Power in a resistor
pages.task: `P(I) = I²R` gives the power `P` for a current `I`. With a 2 Ω resistor, what is `P(3)`?
pages.why: `P(3) = 3² × 2`. `3²` is 9, and `9 × 2` makes 18 W. These dots do not line up: each extra amp adds more watts than the last. That curve is the square, in lesson 3.
